outcome: A July 2026 preprint by Saša Novaković proves that for arithmetic progressions whose step q is polynomially bounded in the length N (q ≲ N^r for any fixed r > 0), the number of squares is N^{1/2+ε} for any ε>0 as N→∞ — matching Rudin's conjectured exponent O(√N) — but only for this restricted class of progressions, not for arbitrary step size, so the general conjecture (Q(N) over all progressions) remains open.
summary: The triage pass (verdict 'none') found nothing post-January-2024 and its searches (generic phrasings of 'Rudin's conjecture' plus year filters) missed this because the relevant work does not use the phrase 'Rudin's conjecture' at all. I found arXiv:2607.15895 ('A comment on the number of k-th powers inside arithmetic progressions', Saša Novaković, submitted 17 July 2026), a 4-page note extending Bourgain and Demeter's 2018 theorem (arXiv:1811.11919) on k-th powers in arithmetic progressions whose step has O(1) divisors. Novaković's Theorem 1.4 shows that for progressions whose step q grows at most polynomially in the length N (q ≲ N^r for any fixed r>0), the number of k-th powers among the first N terms is N^{1/k+ε} for any ε>0 and N large enough; for k=2 this is N^{1/2+ε}, matching Rudin's conjectured O(√N) exponent up to the ε. This restricts the class of arithmetic progressions considered (bounding the step's growth) rather than changing the question, so under §3.1 it is a case of Rudin's conjecture, not a variant: it removes a large swath of arithmetic progressions (all those with sub-polynomial-in-N step, which includes the vast majority of practically considered cases) from the space where the conjecture could still fail, while progressions with faster-growing steps (e.g. the extremal example 24n+1, whose step is a small constant, is actually already covered by the even older Bourgain-Demeter O(1)-divisor case) are the ones for which the full-strength O(√N) bound is not newly established here — the general Q(N) bound over ALL arithmetic progressions (Bombieri-Zannier's O(N^{3/5+o(1)}), still the best known for the fully general case) is untouched. No expert digestion, citation record, or journal acceptance was found for this July 2026 preprint (posted about two months before this research date), so it is not yet 'resolved' — it is a `claimed`-quality single-case result, hence overall problem status `partial` (a case settled, general conjecture still open). No AI system is mentioned anywhere in the paper's introduction, results, or (nonexistent) acknowledgements section; this appears to be conventional solo human mathematics extending a known induction argument, explicitly described by the author as work that 'should be known' but which the author is formally writing up.
competing_reading: One could argue this is closer to a `related problem` / variant rather than a `case`: Bourgain-Demeter's original theorem already covered the O(1)-divisor case, and Novaković's extension to polynomially-bounded steps, while broader, still excludes the general Q(N) problem (unbounded step growth) that Rudin's conjecture is actually about, and the paper itself is presented as an incremental technical comment rather than a targeted attack on Rudin's conjecture (it barely mentions Rudin by name, if at all, in the accessible text). Under a stricter reading, since the extremal near-optimal examples for Q(N) are believed to have small, fixed steps (already covered pre-2024 by Bourgain-Demeter), this new result adds coverage mainly to progressions that were never candidates for the extremal cases anyway, so its practical import for the conjecture as usually discussed is arguably closer to `progress`/`bound` than a genuine `partial` resolution of a case.
what_would_settle_it: A published/peer-reviewed version of arXiv:2607.15895, or an expert digestion (e.g., a citing survey or blog post) explicitly framing the polynomial-step-growth case as settling part of Rudin's conjecture, would confirm the `partial` classification and let it be upgraded toward `resolved` for that case. Absent that, direct confirmation (via the full paper PDF, which I could not cleanly OCR/extract past the abstract and a WebFetch-generated summary) of whether the paper explicitly cites Rudin's conjecture by name would also sharpen the scope call.
